Improving the potential of ﬁfth-generation district heating and cooling 
networks through robust design and operational optimization under future 
energy market and demand uncertainties

Network investments and projected energy prices greatly impact the ﬁnancial viability and environmental 
impact of ﬁfth-generation district heating and cooling (5GDHC) networks. Compared to the previous generation, 
the upfront investment costs in 5GDHC networks are relatively high due to the decentralized energy demand 
and supply of the participating prosumers. The transition to 5GDHC is also hindered by uncertain energy 
markets and the ﬂuctuating energy demands of the prosumers. It makes investors hesitant to commit, even for 
promising business cases. In this work, a framework is presented to assess the economic and environmental 
performance of a 5GDHC business case, based on a multi-objective robust optimization algorithm (MO-RDO), 
to identify the optimal trade-oﬀs between environmental and economic designs. The proposed methodology 
consists of four steps. In the ﬁrst two steps, a speciﬁc business case is modeled, and techno-economic and 
environmental performances are analyzed against uncertain energy markets. In the third step, the techno-
economic and environmental indicator responses are used to develop a data-driven machine-learning model. This 
model oﬀers better computational eﬃciency than a high-ﬁdelity nonlinear model and assesses the most inﬂuential 
parameters driving economic and environmental performance via a global sensitivity analysis. This aids in 
reﬁning the multi-objective robust design optimization (MO-RDO) framework by pinpointing key design variables 
and objectives amid data uncertainties. Additionally, the formulated MO-RDO provides a mix of environmentally 
and economically optimal network designs and operational parameters and highlights the trade-oﬀs between 
them. The designs and trade-oﬀs are evaluated using ﬁnancial metrics like net present value (NPV), return on 
investment, and discounted payback period. These metrics are calculated over the project life, considering the 
initial investment and net savings. For the considered case, the environmental design has a 10% higher investment 
cost compared to the economically optimal solution but reduces total emissions (TE) by 13% and improves 
operational cost savings, which is crucial for better ﬁnancial indicators. The proposed framework aligns with the 
EU transition plan to incorporate waste energy sources and decarbonization paths, estimating only a 3% increase 
in NPV as a risk for the environmentally optimal solution on a ﬁnancial scale.

1.2. Previous work
The development of 5GDHC networks has been explored in various 
research studies. [4]provides  a critical analysis of recent advancements 
from the demonstration phase as well as the literature. Additionally, 
they emphasized cutting-edge approaches for the modeling and opti-
mization of 5GDHC networks. Further, the research on the environmen-
tal and economic performance of the 5GDHC networks is also examined. 
This study’s objectives are to clarify the meaning of 5GDHC networks 
and outline their beneﬁts and drawbacks. According to [9], a study 
was carried out on 40 thermal networks in Europe that could sup-
ply both heating and cooling. Similarly, Volkova et al. [17] highlights 
the challenges of changing a high-temperature network grid to a low-
temperature one due to ﬁnancial limitations. It explains that the time 
it takes to recover the investment made in this transition is longer than 
expected, according to a thorough analysis. Wack etal.[ 18]mentioned  
that the upfront investment is a crucial factor for the DH technology. 
Thus, in [18], a pipe penalization approach for the economic topology 
optimization of District Heating Networks is proposed, which yields the 
optimal net present value of the network.
In Calise et al. [19], a comparative analysis between 4GDHC and 
5GDHC systems is conducted using a SWOT analysis and thermo-
economic evaluation. Each network type employs separate rings to pro-
vide heating and cooling demands. Notably, the 4GDHC system operates 
at elevated network temperature levels, enabling the utilization of high-
grade waste energy from power plants and CHPs. While both network 
types oﬀer signiﬁcant energy savings, their economic and ﬁnancial per-
formance is limited, with payback periods estimated at 16 years for 
4GDHC and 20 years for 5GDHC. The research suggests that 4GDHC 
is optimal for residential districts, whereas 5GDHC is better suited for 
areas with simultaneous heating and cooling demands, oﬀering greater 
proﬁtability and risk mitigation as outlined in the SWOT analysis by 
[9]. Hennessy etal.[ 20]also  highlighted that despite the decentralized 
consumption and production in 5GDHC networks leading to high energy 
costs associated with electricity prices, the Net Present Value (NPV) and 
Discounted Payback Period (DPBP) remain appealing under market con-
ditions.
In Arabkoohsar etal.[ 21], an innovative and cost-eﬀective conﬁgu-
ration of smart energy buildings with energy networks is examined. The 
concept of smart energy buildings involves the integration of new tech-
nologies such as batteries, heat pumps, photovoltaic (PV) panels, pho-
tovoltaic thermal (PVT) systems, and photovoltaic thermal and cooling 
(PVTC) systems ([22,23]). Arabkoohsar et al. [21] developed a com-

In [24], the techno-economic performance of a 5GDHC system for a

electricity is sold to the grid.
In a related study [25], the integration of PV panels with a 5GDHC 
network is analyzed, and a thermo-economic analysis is conducted. The 
study investigates the decentralized generation of heating and cooling 
using heat pumps powered by installed capacities of PV panels. Although 
this conﬁguration oﬀers improved environmental beneﬁts, the ﬁnancial 
analysis reveals a high single project payback period (SPBP) of 33 years. 
The analysis reveals that PV panels only meet 30% of the electricity 
demand due to their intermittent nature. This suggests that integrat-
ing energy storage could alleviate the high SPBP, which is primarily 
driven by the substantial upfront costs associated with installing heat 
pumps and pipes. In [26], a hybrid approach is employed, combining 
physical models with a linear programming method to calculate perfor-
mance metrics such as the levelized cost of energy and diversity factor 
in heating and cooling demands. Importantly, their linear program also 
incorporates investment and associated operational costs of the equip-
ment to maximize the overall NPV of the project. An advanced approach 
to conﬁguring 5GDHC networks by leveraging overlapping building de-
mands in Europe is explored in [27]. The study employs Geographic 
Information System (GIS)-based methods and data sources to analyze 
various regions.
The literature discussed above primarily focused on performance 
analysis without considering uncertainties arising from energy markets 
and network participants’ demands, as elaborated in [3,28]. In [3], over 
10,000 scenarios were examined through Monte Carlo simulations and 
sensitivity analysis. Additionally, Coppitters etal.[ 29],DeMeulenaere  
etal.[ 30]emphasized  that analyzing energy systems using ﬁxed values, 
generic ranges, or precise parameter distributions from the energy mar-
ket often leads to sub-optimal designs that deviate signiﬁcantly from 
reality. To address this issue, a more comprehensive, robust analysis 
incorporating input uncertainties through probability distributions is 
necessary to achieve robust designs.
In a recent study by Zhang et al. [3], a ﬁve-step framework was 
developed, integrating energy system optimization with stochastic simu-
lations, uncertainty analysis, and sensitivity assessment. This framework 
was applied to a small 5GDHC network covering an area of 0.25 km2. 
The performance index of cost-saving probability was chosen to assess 
the potential for constructing 5GDHC networks, revealing that area de-
mand density, overlapping heating and cooling demands, and linear 
demand density are the most sensitive factors. Furthermore, the study 
highlighted the increasingly critical role of investment in Thermal En-
ergy Storage (TES) with the integration of a large share of renewable 
energy. In [15], a systematic method is presented to optimize network 
design and operations amidst uncertain energy demands. The authors 
formulated an optimization cost function that determines the appro-
priate network conﬁguration, speciﬁcally sizing the network pipes, in 
response to uncertain energy demands. Similarly, Akbari etal.[ 31]con-
ducted a related study on designing a network for a local community 
under demand uncertainty, where they assessed the impact of uncer-
tain demands on pipe lengths. In [32], a detailed thermo-hydraulic 
simulation model is constructed using TRANSYS and Fluidit Heat. This 
model is utilized to predict economic performance under the inﬂuence of 
multiple uncertainties generated through Monte Carlo-based simulation 
methods. The study further explores the economic viability of solar-
assisted renewable technologies with 5GDHC systems. The levelized cost 
of heating is selected as a performance indicator when assessing the im-
pact of multiple uncertainties. In their study, Marx etal.[ 33]conducted  
a risk assessment regarding the economic viability of district heating 
(DH) networks in the context of uncertain energy and waste heat avail-
ability. Additionally, they incorporated individual heat supply systems 
into their analysis. They employed a Monte Carlo-based approach to as-
sess the impact of uncertainty on both individual systems and network 
scenarios. Their simulation results revealed that individual systems are 
more signiﬁcantly aﬀected by uncertainties compared to the network 
scenario.
Abokersh et al. [34] developed a systematic framework to perform 
multi-objective optimization using a robust machine learning approach 
to inherent sustainable performance and design of solar-assisted district 
heating systems (SDHS). The framework ﬁrst quantiﬁes the uncertainty 
in the context of SDHS design using global sensitivity analysis followed 
by a heuristic optimization approach. The framework is applied across 
diﬀerent urban community sizes (10, 25, 50, and 100 buildings) situated 
in Madrid. The ﬁndings highlight signiﬁcant enhancements in economic 
and environmental beneﬁts associated with SDHS deployment, partic-
ularly when considering the inclusion of seasonal storage tank (SST) 
construction properties in the optimization process. Abokersh etal.[ 34]
employed a feed-forward neural network approach to construct a meta-
model formulation [35]. In the development process of such models, a 
wide range of training points are introduced through data generation 
(also known as sampling) to verify the accuracy convergence and time 
consumption of the meta-models [36]. In [34], data generation is car-
ried out by utilizing a detailed model in TRANSYS. Finally, a Bayesian 
optimization approach is utilized to enhance the model accuracy and 
conduct sensitivity analysis. Chaudhry etal.[ 37]devised  a framework 
for generic thermodynamic modelingof  5GDHC to analyze the techno-
economic performance of potential business cases. In their framework, 
a systematic strategy is developed to analyze the network that looks 
promising in the preliminary analysis of GIS via uncertainty quantiﬁca-
tion. Therefore, Chaudhry etal.[ 37]evaluated  diﬀerent locations from 
the Flanders region of Belgium against uncertain energy markets and 
proposed a location that shows better indicators against uncertainties.
1.3. Novel contributions
In most previous studies on techno-economic analysis and optimiza-
tion of 5GDHC networks, uncertain variations in energy market scenar-
ios and demands have often been overlooked. Only a few studies, such 
as [3,32–34], have considered the analysis of network design under the 
inﬂuence of uncertainties. For instance, in [32], a Monte Carlo method 
is employed alongside commercial tools like TRANSYS and Fluidit-heat 
to assess the techno-economic performance of 5GDHC networks amidst 
uncertainties. Similarly, [33]c o n d u c t e d a risk assessment concerning 
economic indicators for the network and compared it with individual 
systems. However, neither study performed robust design optimization 
for sustainable operations under uncertain future scenarios. The study 
conducted in [3]is  quite similar to the proposed work by providing ﬁve 
step methodology for uncertainty and sensitivity analysis of the DHC 
systems. For each uncertain scenario, an optimization routine based on 
mixed integer linear programming is used to determine the optimal net-
work design and operational parameters. Subsequently, a probability 
distribution is computed for performance indices such as the levelized 
cost across diﬀerent uncertainties. However, their approach does not 
diﬀerentiate which individual input exerts a greater impact on the per-
formance index; instead, it provides a probability density function (PDF) 
considering the combined eﬀect of all uncertain inputs. Another limita-
tion of the method is the utilization of linear models, which may not ac-

2. Problem statement
The transition to 5GDHC networks faces limitations due to uncertain-
ties in present-day energy markets, constraining investors from making 
decisions even when a particular site appears attractive. These uncer-
tainties encompass factors such as equipment costs, energy prices, and 
CO2 taxes. Moreover, in many 5GDHC networks, energy is exchanged 
among network participants, amplifying the impact of uncertainties 
in participant demands and further restricting the transition. Impor-
tantly, a preliminary analysis using GIS-based approaches, as discussed 
in [27,40–42], is insuﬃcient to address the uncertainty eﬀects related to 
unpredictable energy market behaviorand  ﬂuctuating energy demands.
In this work, a systematic methodology is developed, beginning with 
an analysis of potential locations using simple linear and randomly gen-
erated scenarios to assess the techno-economic performance over the 
project’s life, focusing on ﬁnancial metrics to assess the proﬁtability 
and return on investment. Locations that demonstrate stable KPIs are 
then utilized for robust design optimization, aiming to identify environ-
mentally or economically eﬃcient solutions. These optimized solutions 
are intended to improve overall ﬁnancial metrics while accounting for 
uncertainties that may hinder the transition process. This will assist in-
vestors in making informed decisions based on ﬁnancial analysis.
3. Methodology
This section presents the methods and framework to evaluate and 
optimize the business case for 5GDHC networks in business parks in 
Flanders, Belgium. It considers uncertain energy market and demand 
scenarios. The framework, shown in Fig.1, consists of four steps.
Step 1 explains the thermodynamic modelingframework  section3.1, 
used to analyze locations identiﬁed through a GIS-based approach. It 
also details how prosumers’ energy demands are modeledand  how net-
work equipment is selected. The operational costs of the equipment are 
also discussed. In section3.2and section3.3, the characterization of KPI 
metrics and uncertain input scenarios are explained, respectively.
Step 2 involves risk analysis discussed in section 3.3.1, assessing 
the project’s net present value against uncertain energy market scenar-
ios. Based on Key Performance Indicator (KPI) responses, a preliminary 
techno-economic assessment is conducted to rate each location’s future 
eﬀectiveness in energy demand sharing.
In Step 3, the machine learning approach detailed in section 3.4 is 
applied to analyze over 3000 uncertain input scenarios, identifying the 
key factors that inﬂuence the KPIs of the 5GDHC network. This sim-
pliﬁes the multi-objective optimization process in Step 4, discussed in 
section 3.5, where trade-oﬀs between environmentally and economi-
cally optimal solutions are examined using a computationally eﬃcient 
model based on the PC-Kriging approach.
3.1. 5GDHC network modeling
After conducting the preliminary analysis using a GIS-based ap-
proach in Step 1, the most promising locations are shortlisted. In a 
GIS-based approach, various types of data are uploaded onto platforms 
like QGIS to evaluate the potential of speciﬁc locations. This data may 
include historical information about how people or systems have inter-
acted, current network layouts of utilities like gas and electricity, basic 
information about the landscape, and weather data. The shortlisted sites 
are then further analyzed in Step 2 using the Python-based Heat Distri-
bution System Simulator (HDSS) for detailed design.

6. Conclusion
In this study, a robust design and optimization framework was pre-
sented to optimize the design parameters of a 5GDHC network under 
the inﬂuence of uncertain energy markets and the energy supplies and 
demands of the participating prosumers. 2000 uncertain scenarios are 
generated for a potential 5GDHC business case, and an ML is employed 
on a uniformly distributed input and output data set. The performance 
of the ML model is analyzed in comparison with the data set, which has 
been generated from a Python-based high-ﬁdelity model. In general, al-
most 90% linear agreement between the high-ﬁdelity model and ML 
model holds for CAPEXo and TE. As a result, the ML model replaces 
the computationally ineﬃcient model of the 5GDHC network with a 
simple surrogate. Before solving the complex formulated multi-objective 
robust design optimization problem (MO-RDO), the proposed ML model 
identiﬁes critical design variables in the presence of numerous uncertain 
inputs from energy markets and the uncertain thermal properties of par-
ticipants. This has been accomplished by performing global sensitivity 
analysis, yielding Sobol’s indices to quantify the impact of each input 
on output.
For the considered case study, high Sobol’s indices for gas prices in-
dicate a greater impact than electricity prices, suggesting that lower gas 
prices could undermine the 5GDHC business case. Additionally, Sobol’s 
analysis identiﬁes which buildings most signiﬁcantly aﬀect the network 
KPIs due to variations in demand and thermal characteristics. Accord-
ing to Sobol’s analysis, only 6 from the considered 24 inputs have a 
high impact. At the same time, only 3 of the 6 high Sobol’s inputs are 
considered for the MO-RDO, being the supply (𝑇h) and return (𝑇c) tem-
perature of the network and the diameter of the network pipes to the 
building with high Sobol’s. Consequently, the proposed methodology 
reduced the computational complexity of the optimization problem by 
systematically reducing the number of design variables for large net-
works.
The overall objective of the proposed methodology is to maximize 
the ﬁnancial metrics such as NPV. The components of NPV, as given 
in eq.(40), are optimized along with the objective to reduce the TE in 
the presence of uncertainties. This transforms the network optimization 
problem into MO-RDO of the form eq.(54). The optimization framework 
selects the best combination of decision variables that can optimize the 
objectives as given in eq. (54). Each combination represents a variety 
of optimal designs (environmentally optimal or economically optimal) 
and trade-oﬀs that form a Pareto frontier. In contrast to the economically 
optimal design, the environmental design had a 10% higher investment 
cost but reduced TE by 13% and improved net savings. Only a 3% in-
crease in NPV is estimated as a risk for the environmentally optimal 
solution on a ﬁnancial scale. Thus, following the EU energy policy for 
CO2 reduction, the environmental design anticipates only a 3% reduc-
tion in NPV over the project life, despite higher investment costs and 
uncertain energy markets.
The methodology enhances ﬂexibility in identifying key uncertain 
input parameters and evaluating the robustness of critical performance 
indicators, addressing the limitations of current GIS-based approaches.
